To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the disease states (dysplastic and hyper plasic tissues) of colon biopsied samples can be distinguished effectively with Fourier transform infrared spectroscopic im aging without eliminating the Mie scattering effect and that the disease states can be distinguished effectively by machine learning without using C–H stretching or amide I bands.

C–H stretching (3000–2800 cm−1) and amide I (1700–1600 cm−1, 1650 cm−1 band) bands are of little or no significance in the discrimination of different stages of colorectal malignancy, based upon Gini importance values.

the disease state of colon tissues could be distinguished effectively with the use of machine learning algorithms without eliminating Mie scattering effect and the most significant bands for the distinction between different colon tissues are located in the fingerprint region between 1500–1000 cm− 1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of the significance of amides I and II bands and the C–H stretching band of colon tissues in diagnostic applications with FTIR spectroscopic imaging.
the development of a Fourier transform infrared (FIR) imaging system that can be used to detect colon cancer.
the evaluation of the importance of amide I band and C–H bands in the diagnostic applications of FTIR spectroscopic imaging of human colon biopsies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the C–H stretching region is of no significance in the discrimination of colon tissue stages, and that the most significant region is between 1000 and 1500 cm−1, which is the fingerprint region of infrared spectra, excluding the contribution of amides I and II.
C–H stretch and amide I are not important for the discrimination of the disease states, but the fingerprint region of colon tissue is very significant for the discrimination.

C–H bands and amide I are of no importance in the classification of colon malignancy and that the disease states can be distinguished effectively in the fingerprint region without elimination of the scattering effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that it is possible to classify the disease state of colon tissues by FTIR spectroscopic imaging.
we have demonstrated that the amide I and the C–H stretching band of colon biopsied tissues are not of importance in the classification of colon malignancy.
FTIR spectroscopic imaging of human colon biopsies in transmission combined with supervised machine learning can be a powerful tool to distinguish different stages of colon cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
C–H and amide I stretching bands are of little significance in the classification and diagnosis of colon cancer.
the C–H stretching region and amide I band are of little to almost no significance in the diagnosis of colon malignancies, as the Gini importance of random forest shows.

the important differences that distinguish between the different stages of colon cancer are within the fingerprint region, and the contribution of the amide I and amide II bands to the classification is negligible.
